processing: Typical of Fenghuang Dancong: sun-withered, shaken and rested to partial oxidation, fired, rolled and dried or lightly roasted.
harvest_season: As with most Fenghuang Dancong, spring is the main picking.
appearance_dry: Tight, straight strips, dark brown and oily in sheen.
appearance_wet: Typically slender leaves with reddened edges, in keeping with the lanceolate leaf of this small-leaf bush.
taste_profile: A clear, high aroma with florals, and a mellow, sweet, fresh taste with a distinct Dancong character.

brewing.notes: As with other Dancong, keep steeps short. Try a bag again at the end of the year, when the aroma is said to come back.

vintage_note: Usually sold by spring harvest, as with other Dancong. A Chinese guide says the finished tea regains its fragrance toward the year's end (fan chun), so a spring lot drunk in winter is worth trying. True old-tree material can only be scarce, so most offered is likely from propagated plants.
description:
Gong Xiang, 'tribute aroma', is listed among the famous bushes of Wudong in the Fenghuang range. One Chinese guide puts its mother bush in Xiashushan, a garden in Zhongxinyan village, at roughly 1,000 metres, and gives its age as more than 350 years.

The bush is a small-leaf, small-arbor type with spreading branches and lanceolate leaves. It has been propagated on a small scale by cuttings and grafting, and its offspring are fairly widely planted on the high ground of Wudong.

The finished tea is described as tight, straight and dark, with a bright orange-yellow liquor, a high, clear floral aroma and a sweet, fresh taste. Brew it as you would other Dancong, with quick pours and not too much leaf.

The same guide reports that the aroma comes back around the end of the year. When buying, ask whether the leaf is from old bushes or from their offspring, because the price should differ a lot.
history: The tree's age of over 350 years comes from a Chinese guide to the famous bushes of Wudong, and it has not been independently confirmed. Offspring grown from cuttings and grafts spread across the high Wudong gardens. The name suggests tribute, but little is documented about any actual tribute use, so treat it as a name and not as history.
